senses.definition: A keen-edged knife of peculiar shape, used in shaving the hair from the face or other parts of the body.
Any tool or instrument designed for shaving.

quotes.text: These are fellows who shun the three-, four- and five-blade contraptions and canned goops for an older mode of shaving that they insist remains the ideal: a straight razor or a safety razor with a double-edged blade, and a fine English cream lathered and applied with a badger-hair brush.
quotes.reference: 2007 July 1, Jake Mooney, “For Aficionados of Shaving, la Crème de la Crème”, in The New York Times:

quotes.text: The box was jam packed full o' gifts for each manjack of us: razors, aftershave, toothbrushes, an' books.
quotes.reference: 2013, Robert L. Buyer, Ursula T. Coute, Following the North Star, page 26:

senses.definition: The sharp tusk of a wild boar.
(philosophy) A conceptual device that allows one to shave away unlikely explanations for a phenomenon.

quotes.text: He thought likewise, that what with razoring and tanning, and the change of his clothes, he was not likely to be recognised.
quotes.reference: 1868, George MacDonald, chapter 6, in Guild Court, volume 3, London: Hurst & Blackett, page 137:

quotes.text: Lord Tywin did not believe in half measures. He razored his lip and chin as well, but kept his side-whiskers, two great thickets of wiry golden hair that covered most of his cheeks from ear to jaw.
quotes.reference: 1996, George R. R. Martin, “Tyrion”, in A Game of Thrones, New York: Bantam, published 2016, page 641:

quotes.text: He might be busy examining the advertisements for prostitutes stuck up in a São Paulo phone booth, or maybe getting his ear hairs razored off at a barber shop in Vietnam.
